Frum: Well, what I remember, that’s actually maybe one of my most vivid memories of the day, is stepping out of that building. And Washington is deserted, and there’s yellow tape everywhere marking off the streets, and there’s the National Guard and armored personnel carriers everywhere.

But the flags are still flying. They’ll be lowered the next—I remember thinking, They will be lowered tomorrow. But tonight they’re high, and they’re lit up. And this capital is that ghostly beauty of Washington at night, one of the most, maybe the most, beautiful city in America at night. And there are armored personnel everywhere; there are military everywhere.

And you may not share the view—this is my view, and I won’t attribute it to you. But if you’ve been to Washington recently, and you’ve had feelings about seeing armed men in the streets of the nation’s capital, and they seem like an unwelcome force, like something imposed from outside, just imagine the opposite. The farthest of looking at it, and saying, This is the armed forces of the United States, here to protect the nation’s capital. Thank God they’re here; how proud we are of them. How much we admire them; how grateful we are.

I remember later, just to flash ahead, talking to a National Guard commander saying that one of his biggest problems with his deployment in Washington was managing his troops’ weight, because local merchants kept bringing them donuts and cake and coffee and cookies. And after, like, the third round he had to say, No, no more cookies. No more cookies.

McConnell: Well, and you remember the president said the following week, just meditating on that day, and as you were noting—it was the perfect, perfect day. And then, remember the National Book Festival had been on the 8th. Saturday the 8th on the Mall; I think the 8th and 9th. And the National Book Festival would just spread out on the Mall, the lawn of the Library of Congress. People walking in and out of the Library of Congress building. And it was just free movement. And I think the president and Mrs. Bush went up there at one point and wandered around among the book festival.

And anyway, what the president said after the events—he said, Night fell on a different world.

Frum: Yeah. So it’s about 8:00 at night. We get into the White House. Again, and it’s a different White House. Because the security—although there was security before 9/11, a lot of security—it was different after. And it was already, it was instantly different.

So we didn’t go watch the president speak, which is what I think we normally would’ve done. Again, there were just many more barriers to moving around inside. And the president spoke to the nation, but still in a way that was a little punch drunk, in my opinion.

And I looked this up later. So, after the firing on Fort Sumter, President Lincoln’s first communication to the nation is a written proclamation that he issued three days after the firing on Fort Sumter. And after the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Roosevelt’s first communication to the nation was his Day of Infamy speech. But Pearl Harbor was struck at dawn Hawaii time, which on Sunday, which is about midday Washington time Sunday. And the president spoke first thing Monday. So however many hours that is before the first communication. In—it’s not yet the social-media age, but it’s the cable-TV age, and the president has to speak the same day, immediately. And in a way, there isn’t really time. That isn’t enough time to organize what you’re going to say. And so even the 8:00 speech struck me as not the right tone, not the right message exactly.

McConnell: Well, and then it was Monday the 17th where we got the assignment to do the speech to Congress on Thursday. And that was, of course, that would be then September 20th. It was nine days after the events in question. And if you look at history, it feels like a long time. But he did have the speech at the National Cathedral on Friday, and the radio address. Which I don’t even remember what that—

Frum: Well, I want to put a break—again, I want to slow down here a little bit, because here are the things I remember that are signal events before the speech to Congress.

There’s the speech to the National Cathedral, as you said, which was, I thought, so—that was beautiful. This is not my own work. I’ll say, because my portfolio was domestic and economic, so I was spending all my time on, like, the stock market and the reopening of the airlines. So the speeches I’m about to praise, I had nothing to do with. That beautiful speech at the National Cathedral, which I think you and Scully mostly wrote. And then he went to New York to speak at Ground Zero. And that famous moment, “I can hear you,” that was, as far as I’m aware, completely improvised in the moment. And then—and I think this is the thing, I think, people don’t remember enough—that he went to the Washington mosque on Massachusetts Avenue, I think, again, before the speech to Congress. And stood with dignitaries local and national, and made a speech for tolerance.

And I just want to stress this point, because there is a lot of misremembering and I think a lot of misinformation about what it was like to belong to the American Muslim community after 9/11. There were a flurry of hate attacks after 9/11, in the immediate aftermath of 9/11. I remember, in fact, I think three of them were murders. Two of the murders were carried out by the same person. And the three victims—only one of the three was Muslim; one was Sikh, and one was South Asian of non-Muslim background. And then many other incidents of harassment and intimidation and insult and vandalism. But the president was so forceful condemning it that that flurry of hate-crime incidents—and three of them murders in the immediate aftermath—was quickly stopped.

And there is a dramatic drop-off between, after the month of September into October. I think the killings were in September and October. By January of 2002, the FBI is recording a steep drop, I think, of hate-crime incidents, from that last half of 2001. And that the leadership of President Bush and people like him really made an important difference in creating an atmosphere of tolerance and respect that is not as remembered as well as it should be.

McConnell: Well, that’s a nice point, David. And this is a great country, and no patriot is going to want to harm an innocent, unsuspecting person in response to something like this. I mean, this is the horror of 9/11, is that very thing: harming innocent, unsuspecting people. And President Bush in that sense spoke for the best in our country and brought out the best, as I like to think he always did, and I know that he tried to do.

Frum: Well, again, to conjure it up, so—President Bush is kind of an accidental president in a way. He lost the popular vote in the election of 2000. He becomes president, he wins the electoral vote, and everything teeters on the state of Florida, where, on a few dozen votes in the state of Florida—because in those days, every county got to design its own ballot, and many of the counties did a bad job. And there was recount upon recount, and tremendous ill feeling about it. And it left behind, I think, a shadow. I know he spent a lot of the first half of 2001 trying to find ways to broaden his support. There is an emphasis on education as an early initiative, because that had broad bipartisan support. You could pass it with big majorities of both Republicans and Democrats in both houses of Congress.

But still, there was a question mark over his presidency up to that moment. And I think there was this feeling of—would he measure up? Could this accidental president be someone who could speak for the nation after 9/11?

McConnell: Well, that’s right. And I remember Bob Dole candidly said, some months after that, he said—I think he was talking about September 14th, when Bush was on that flattened fire truck in New York City with the bullhorn, and didn’t even know he was expected to speak and had nothing prepared for him. And then had one of the iconic moments of his presidency—and Bob Dole said, that was like a second inauguration. (Laughs.) And it really was the man meeting his moment, and people getting a sense of him that they really hadn’t had or allowed. Or, in the case of many Americans, allowed themselves to have at that time.

Frum: Well, on his way to that moment, he landed in New York, and he was taken in a car to Lower Manhattan. And the emergency workers there are the firefighters, and a lot of, not onlookers because the area’s closed to the public, but there were a lot of people there. And they’re all cheering and waving and clapping and greeting him enthusiastically. And Mayor Giuliani, who was in the car with Bush—and Mayor Giuliani was a very different man in 9/11 from the man he is now—and I later heard that he had said to the president, You see all these people cheering for you? Not one of them voted for you.

McConnell: Well, and President Bush—you’ve heard him tell the story, David, and he repeated it in his book. He has a strong emotional memory of just one guy in a hard hat standing on a mound of rubble, making eye contact with him, and pointing his finger and said, “Don’t you let me down.”

Frum: (Laughs.)

McConnell: And it really, really touched his heart and stays with him to this day.

Frum: All right. So we have just a few minutes left. I want to flash forward; now look back on this from the perspective of 25 years. How did the country do? How did the Bush administration do? What did we get right? What did we get wrong? Do you have thoughts looking backward from a perspective of a quarter century on 9/11, and what it meant and what it led to?

McConnell: Nothing deep or profound. I grew up in the ’70s and ’80s. I remember once when I was about nine or 10 years old—I grew up in a town of 500 people in northern Wisconsin, and I have this memory of walking with one of my little friends around this little town on a summer day. And we agreed that we were probably never going to see a war in our lifetimes, because people, they don’t do this anymore. You know what I mean? That’s how things felt in the mid- to late ’70s. People aren’t going to fight wars anymore, big tanks and armies and all this stuff. And we just looked ahead to a future where that kind of tragedy and sorrow just wouldn’t fall on the human race like it used to. This is, you know, innocent kid stuff, right?

And the ’80s were pretty quiet. And you had the Cold War, but it’s a pretty, pretty quiet decade when you think about it. And so the point is—when 9/11 happened, that was very jarring for me, as it was for everybody. And you get this sense that the world—we might see a lot of things like this from now on, and we might see a lot of things like this inside the United States. That was my biggest fear, that the United States would, having found itself vulnerable that day, would continue to be. I didn’t think we had to be, but I was afraid that we might be.

And so when I look back, I think mainly of the president you and I worked for, and the responsibilities that we had. And there’s only so much that speechwriters can do. There’s only so much that’s on the page, and the rest is up to him. And when he did such a great job in those moments, it’s really because of him and the kind of man he was. And this was, as I said before, a man meeting his moment. And our country has not descended into the kind of fright and vulnerability that many of us feared could happen, and that’s not by accident. A lot of good decisions were made; a lot of difficult decisions were made that kept us safe. We could talk about any number of particulars and wars and things of that nature that have come since.

But by and large, I look back on that time as a pivotal point, a moment of great decision. And things were handled well by the people in power.

Frum: I will have a somewhat different view, which I’ll present on a later occasion. I’ll say just one thing as I think back on it. I think there are many might-have-beens in history, and I’m not a big believer in these alternative scenarios, because usually things that have big consequences don’t have happenstance causes. If the guns firing at Fort Sumter had missed, the Civil War would still have happened.

But one I do think about is, if [Osama] bin Laden had not got away in Tora Bora in December of 2001, if the United States and Britain and the many other allies who were there, and the Afghan partners of the United States—if they had succeeded in cornering him and killing him in Tora Bora at the end of 2001, would we have had the quarter century of wars in the Middle East that have since happened? His getting away caused an upping of the ante of American policy. The United States had to do something, and had failed to do in December 2001 the most necessary and logical and demanded thing. And so, sometimes when you fail to solve a problem, you redefine the problem to make the problem bigger.

It’s September 11th, 2026. The United States is at war with Iran; American troops have been engaged in anti-terrorist and counterterrorist operations all over the planet for a quarter century. The death toll has been high for Americans, and even higher for others. And I think that 9/11 of 2001 put us on this path. There was an exit in December of 2001, and we didn’t take the exit. We missed the exit. Not through anyone’s fault, or not through anyone’s intention. Maybe somebody’s fault. Not through anyone’s intention. We missed the exit, and here we are. And we’ll be talking about that more in the coming weeks.

And John, I thank you so much. Not only did I spend that day with you, I remember also very vividly spending my last day at the White House with you. We had lunch that day, and I remember going with you to the big bow in the South Lawn, the iron fence, and looking out and thinking, All my life I’ve wanted to look into this fence. I’ve had a year and a half of looking out of the fence, and now I’m looking out of it for the last time, with my good friend McConnell by my side. And for the rest of my life, I’ll be back to looking inside and trying to make sense of this with everyone else’s eyes of looking in.

But you, you’ve spent so much of your life inside, and your knowledge is so profound, and your heart is so big, and it was an honor to work with you and to be your friend.

McConnell: Thank you, David. It was an honor to be your colleague as well. It was a great time, and we’re so privileged to have had that experience.

Frum: Bye-bye.

McConnell: Thank you.

[Music]

Frum: Thanks so much to my friend John McConnell for joining me today on The David Frum Show. This week’s book is also a contemplation of terrorism, but in this case, a contemplation of homegrown, domestic American terrorism. The book is American Pastoral by Philip Roth, published in 1997. In my opinion, probably his greatest novel.

American Pastoral tells a story of an American Jew whose daughter gets mixed up in extremist activity. The novel is narrated by a man named Nathan Zuckerman, who’s Roth’s recurring literary alter ego. And Nathan Zuckerman tells a story of his childhood friend, Seymour “The Swede” Levov, a golden-boy athlete from Zuckerman and Roth’s hometown of Newark, New Jersey. The Swede seems to have it all. He’s a former high-school sports star. He marries a Miss New Jersey. He takes over his father’s successful glove-manufacturing business, and he settles into an idyllic life in rural Old Rimrock, New Jersey. He has one child, an adored daughter named Merry, M-E-R-R-Y.

Merry becomes increasingly politically outspoken in the course of the 1960s, when the novel is set. She gets involved in radical causes. She becomes increasingly dogmatic. Merry has a speech impediment, and somehow that concentrates her rage into forms of action that are beyond speech. And ultimately, that expressed itself when, in order to oppose the Vietnam War, Merry plants a bomb in the local post office that kills a local doctor. Merry then disappears, goes underground, and The Swede spends years looking for her.

When he finally tracks her down, she’s back in Newark, New Jersey, living in terrible filth and squalor, and she has converted to a form of ultra-pacifism. She becomes a Jain, J-A-I-N, a religion from India that is so opposed to violence that it refuses to kill even an insect. And The Swede has to contemplate how his beloved daughter could swing from one extreme of murder to this other extreme of pacifism almost beyond reason.

The Swede, who’s had this perfect life—sheltered from everything, coasting on inherited prosperity and success on an American dream in a country that has been a golden land for Jews like himself—he has to confront this eruption of what Roth calls “the American berserk,” the country’s capacity to burst out from anybody’s planned order into these forms of strange, bizarre personal violence.

Roth is here describing something very real. I mean, I went through, did a quick scroll through incidents that reminded me of the story of Merry Levov—of privileged people, people at every American advantage who lash out, who would adopt some scheme of or some personal ideology of extremist hate, and then lash out in violence against others. There’s so many examples of this. Let me just mention a few that just come to mind in the course of an ordinary search.

Remember Elliot Rodger? Elliot Rodger was the son of a Hollywood director. He grew up in very comfortable circumstances. He developed this ideology of misogyny; incel, I think, is the term. Misogyny, violent hatred to women. He killed six people and wounded 14 in a rampage, leaving behind a manifesto justifying what he did.

Or Patrick Crusius. He was the man who turned a weapon on a parking lot in El Paso to kill 23 people, motivated by his “Great Replacement,” anti-immigrant ideology. He also acted alone, and he also had a comfortable middle-class upbringing in Dallas, Texas.

Or Luigi Mangione—this is a perfect example of this—who comes from a prominent family in Maryland, and he gunned down an insurance executive in New York City. Again, for some crazy, bizarre ideological reason all his own, that unfortunately has found resonance in some of the more malicious corners of online life.

Or Ayman Mohamed Ghazali; I’ve talked about him before. He’s the Lebanese immigrant who settled in Michigan, was given the opportunity to make a life for himself in America, given the amazing gift of American citizenship, and instead took guns to Temple Israel in West Bloomfield.

You know, these people all have motives. They may be diagnosable as having some kind of mental illness, but they’re not so delusional as not to understand what they’re doing. But they’re acting on some script, some sense of grievance—the American berserk that Roth talks about—that pushes them in these directions.

And notice something else. They all have these remarkable resources and freedom. They have the resources to acquire weapons, and they have the freedom to conduct their work without surveillance. There are many societies in which people like this would be caught early because they lived in more of a surveillance state. Americans have freedom, resources. They have the ability to become whoever they are. And for most of us, the ability to become whoever we are is a great gift. It allows us to realize ourselves in all kinds of ways, in ways that people could not realize themselves even in countries that are comparably free but are not as supremely abundant and affluent as the United States.

But when you’re given the right to be who you are, that reveals something in some people that is berserk, that is bad. It allows, it gives you more scope to be indulged in wickedness and cruelty and hatefulness, to come up with some crazy set of ideas all your own, or that link in some other way. And to act out against your fellows in ways that bring hurt and harm and sorrow and suffering to the human species.

America gives all of us the means to be ourselves, and the question we all face is: Who will we be?

That’s it for this week’s episode of The David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching. As ever, please, the best way to support the work of the show, if you can, is by subscribing to The Atlantic. That helps me and all of my colleagues. Please also consider subscribing to our YouTube channel, or whatever social-media channel you enjoy the program on. Share it with others, and spread the word. See you next week on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

entries.title: The Inside Story of What Happened at Stars and Stripes
entries.summary: For generations, the newspaper has served American military families. That work must continue. And it must remain editorially independent.
entries.content:
For generations, the newspaper has served American military families. That work must continue. And it must remain editorially independent.

A “chicken plate,” in military parlance, is a protective shield used in a variety of combat situations. During the Vietnam War, chicken plates were inserted into vests—they are resistant against small-arms fire, but they’re also bulky and hot. So some pilots sat on them instead, which had the added benefit of providing protection against bullets that came from below.

I first encountered another type of chicken plate in Iraq, where I was embedded with a convoy of American service members patrolling outside of Tikrit.

On this particular morning, I sat alongside three soldiers inside an up-armored Humvee while a gunner manned the turret. But that gunner—James Murphy, a sergeant from New Jersey—wasn’t sitting in his sling, which was little more than a seat-belt strap hooked between two sides of the turret. If he sat down, the chicken plate would block his view. This left Murphy with a choice: stand up for hours and expose his head and chest, or remain behind the plate’s limited protection and endanger the convoy by missing a threat.

For the dozen or so gunners I spoke with, the choice was clear. Two of them removed the chicken plate entirely for a better view.

The military had no specific data on gunner casualties or whether the chicken plates were preventing them. Yet an Army general in Iraq was asking his staff why they were losing so many gunners. One officer I spoke with at the time told me that the answer was obvious the moment someone stood in the turret.

I reported a series of stories on gunners for Stars and Stripes, a newspaper with a long history of editorial independence despite being housed within the Department of Defense. A few weeks later, after returning to my home at the time—a room at the bachelor officers’ quarters on a Marine Corps base in Okinawa—I received a message from our Pentagon beat reporter, who told me that military officials had read the series and were fast-tracking improved equipment for deployment. They’d found a way to help protect the gunners without blocking their view from the turret.

I don’t want to overstate my role. At least some military officials were aware of the issue and had been testing prototypes for better shields. But many of the soldiers weren’t willing to discuss with senior leaders the specifics of what they needed, out of concern that they’d be viewed as complaining. I’m grateful that they trusted me enough to tell their stories.

Looking back now, what feels remarkable isn’t the lack of proper equipment. It’s the way the Pentagon was willing to take independent journalism that spotlighted deficiencies and use it to improve conditions for service members.

Uniformed military leaders have not lost the means to analyze and act on useful journalism. But publicly denouncing the reporting or the news outlet makes it far less likely that they will. Attacking people for telling the truth creates a chilling effect for truth tellers—including those who are themselves in the military.

The best journalism unearths information that complex bureaucracies overlook or suppress, intentionally or not. When leaders treat asking tough questions and reporting uncomfortable facts as disloyalty, they devalue a tool that can help them fix crucial problems.

The danger in this devaluation is immense, especially now; it comes as U.S. service members are once again fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon hasn’t held a press briefing on combat operations in Iran since May 5. The Correspondents’ Corridor, where reporters worked inside the Pentagon for decades, is closed while court appeals continue on press-access restrictions. The New York Times is suing the Pentagon on First Amendment grounds, arguing that the Pentagon’s attempts to prevent independent reporting are clearly unconstitutional. (I should disclose that I, too, am suing the Pentagon. I was fired after I said in an appearance on CBS News that my personal red line would be if the Pentagon ever instructed me not to publish a perfectly accurate story. It is telling that I am being fired for describing the most anodyne of journalistic ethics, a position that any self-respecting reporter in any free society would hold, and that the Pentagon interpreted as insubordination.)

Stars and Stripes has its roots in the Civil War, when Union soldiers took over a printing press in Bloomfield, Missouri. The paper was revived during World War I under General John “Black Jack” Pershing and has published continuously since 1942, when General George C. Marshall recognized the value it provided troops and aimed to follow Pershing’s example. “No official control was ever exercised over the matter which went into” Stars and Stripes, Marshall said of the WWI edition.

It didn’t take long for that editorial freedom to be challenged. General George Patton complained about the “Willie and Joe” cartoonist Bill Mauldin’s depictions of soldiers as they often appeared—tired and dirty. (Mauldin would have known; he was himself a soldier.) But General Dwight Eisenhower rejected Patton’s drive to control the reporting itself. “It is the soldier’s paper,” he said, “and we won’t interfere,” according to the historian Stephen Ambrose’s foreword in a book by Mauldin, whose wartime cartoons earned him the 1945 Pulitzer Prize.

The newspaper continued to operate overseas after World War II, hiring civilian journalists to work alongside service members. But attempts at curtailing Stripes’ independence periodically arose. Congress documented occasional pressures in the 1960s. In the ’80s, a General Accounting Office report to Congress found conclusive evidence of censorship, and pointed out the “inherent cultural conflict” between the First Amendment mission and the military’s own.

Those findings led the House Armed Services Committee to direct the Pentagon to establish an ombudsman, responsible to Congress, who would monitor the free flow of information to service members through Stars and Stripes. And in 1993, a Defense Department directive affirmed that Stars and Stripes is editorially independent of the military chain of command. A subsequent federal regulation added to those protections.

In 2020, the Pentagon proposed cutting all funding to Stars and Stripes, after the department’s comptroller stated that it is “probably not the best way that we communicate any longer.” The idea drew a bipartisan rebuke in Congress. The White House agreed with the lawmakers, and Stripes lived on.

Last November, I moved to Washington, D.C., to accept the editor-in-chief job at the paper, where I’d already been serving as Europe and Middle East chief, based near Ramstein Air Base, in Germany.

Two months later, the Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell fired a broadside at Stars and Stripes. On January 15, he posted on X that the news organization must be rid of “woke distractions that syphon morale.”

The same day, the Pentagon revoked the federal regulation it had established in 1994, calling it unnecessary. The Daily Wire reported that half of all Stripes content would come from the military’s public-affairs team, and that civilian reporters would be replaced by military members. When Stars and Stripes reporters called the Pentagon press office for comment and clarification, they received nothing more than a referral to the tweet and the Daily Wire story.

On February 28, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, killing Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The first Stars and Stripes story came from a wire service, because there aren’t any Stripes reporters inside Iran. But within hours, we had half a dozen stories focused on the U.S. military bases in the region and the people there. In Bahrain, civilians were given the order to evacuate an hour after missiles began falling on the headquarters base of the U.S. Fifth Fleet.

The coverage drew millions of readers, and a video shot by one of our active-duty reporters of a plume rising over the Navy base was viewed all over the world. We worked hard on covering the Iran conflict and thought little of that January tweet—that is, until a Pentagon memo came in mid-March.

The memo simultaneously affirmed our independence and added restrictions. That wire-service story from Iran was now forbidden, along with any other paid wire-service news. So were the comics, of all things. Our publishing decisions would be subject to “good order and discipline”—a line borrowed from the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Our military reporters, who function as interns and receive mentorship from seasoned civilian journalists, now had to wonder whether writing a story might land them in legal jeopardy.

I told military reporters who were worried that a story might hurt their career to let us know, and we’d reassign it. Meanwhile, the staff never compromised on their ethics and values. They reported fairly and accurately and, when called for, held power to account.

The ombudsman wrote a column that assailed the news restrictions, in keeping with the duties set by Congress. Two weeks later, the Defense Department fired her.

By the time I sat down with CBS’s David Martin in late June, I had spoken with no fewer than 16 news outlets and authors about Stars and Stripes. Martin asked me about the “woke distractions” referenced in the January tweet and I answered honestly—that the Pentagon had never explained to us what that meant.

Martin also asked whether I had a personal red line when it came to press restrictions, and I said that I did. If the Pentagon were to say, “Don’t run a perfectly accurate story. Run this instead. Here it is, written by the Pentagon. That would be a red line.”

My response to hypothetical censorship was consistent with what military leaders have said for more than a century, and with the Defense Department’s own directive barring censorship and news management. It is also consistent with basic journalistic ethics: Without editorial independence, journalists cannot uphold their duty to the public.

As part of the CBS interview, the Middle East correspondent Lara Korte stated that she worked for Stars and Stripes, not the Pentagon. She made the distinction to underscore her independence, which is essential to credibility. I learned approximately a week later that the Pentagon press office wasn’t happy about the interview, but that was all I heard.

On August 12, seven weeks after the CBS interview, the Pentagon sent notices of proposed separation for Korte and me to Stripes’ publisher, Max Lederer, and told him to sign them.

Lederer was an Airborne soldier turned Army attorney who was awarded the Bronze Star before he joined Stars and Stripes. He worked his way up through business operations to serve for two decades as publisher.

He reviewed the separation notices and pointed out legal and ethical inconsistencies. Those concerns were dismissed. Rather than sign the notices, he submitted his resignation. (They fired him instead.)

On August 21, the three of us received the separation notices, which listed insubordination as the primary charge. The notices issued to Korte and me cited our CBS comments but didn’t state which order we were purportedly disobeying. Lederer’s firing was for not signing the documents in the first place.

That same day, the Pentagon replaced the directive issued in 1993. Among other things, it bars comics deemed editorial in nature and prevents reporters from using the Freedom of Information Act on behalf of the news organization. I can’t think of another American media outlet with the same restriction.

About an hour after we received our separation notices, the military deputy to the publisher, who’d arrived two weeks earlier, ordered a 10-page document to be published on Stripes.com within 30 minutes. The document stated that Stripes would continue to run independent journalism and that “it is time to take them at their word,” referring to the Pentagon.

I do take them at their word. All of the words they’ve put out since January, along with their actions. The Pentagon has articulated a remarkably narrow view of press freedom. The government may stop short of censoring an individual story. But it will seek to fire newsroom leaders for opposing the replacement of accurate reporting with press releases. It will strip an organization of basic reporting tools it deems unnecessary or distasteful. And it will discredit the source of the reporting if a story is perceived as unflattering to the president or his secretary of defense.

The press isn’t a perfect institution. A global 2026 Reuters Institute survey found that the percentage of people who report trusting the news dropped to the lowest level since Reuters began asking the question in 2015; in the U.S., only 25 percent of Americans said that they trust the news most of the time. Whatever combination of press failures and partisanship produced this decline, public trust has eroded. And it’s that erosion that has made it much easier for officials to delegitimize accurate, balanced journalism.

Reporters, like anyone, make mistakes, but ethical journalism remains fundamentally useful to government and to the citizens who hold it accountable. People in large organizations—the U.S. military included—often avoid delivering bad news for fear of appearing to oppose a leader’s plans. Independent reporting moves information forward, but only if sources know they’ll be able to speak with journalists without fear of reprisal, and if they believe that leaders are open to reacting to criticism like professionals.

That’s what happened in Iraq. The gunners knew what they needed to do their job safely. They didn’t want to be viewed as complainers. Independent journalism sent the message to those who needed to hear it.

*Image sources: Jim Watson / AFP / Getty; Win McNamee / Getty; Lyalya Go / Getty; HUM Images / Getty; Toronto Star Archives / Getty; Universal History Archive / Getty; Library of Congress.

As pressures bore down on an American institution, its secretary held firm.

Americans may not realize for many years just how lucky they were that Lonnie G. Bunch III led the Smithsonian Institution from 2019 to 2026. Bunch has announced that he will step down at the end of this year. He insists that the timing is his own, and we should do him the honor of believing him—notwithstanding the immense pressure the administration has applied to the Smithsonian generally and Bunch personally since Donald Trump returned to office last year.

Bunch, 73, would likely have chosen to retire earlier if not for his sense of duty—his conviction (which few dispute) that he was the best person to guide the Smithsonian through a turbulent period. The Smithsonian is the world’s largest museum, education, and research complex. It’s also “part of the glue,” as Bunch himself said shortly after taking office, “that holds the country together.”

Since his appointment as the Smithsonian’s top official—its 14th secretary and the first historian and Black man to hold the position—in June 2019, Bunch has been the glue holding the Smithsonian together. Through a combination of principled stances and deft political skills, he has kept the sprawling institution on mission and aligned with its public. Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said in a statement that Bunch has “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian has “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision, and leadership.”

Bunch is a fighter, but a smart one. He has often struck me as a master of institutional jiu-jitsu—a leader who knows instinctively when to hold the line, when to yield, and how to convert yielding to the advantage of the institution he has done so much to advance and protect. “When you’re Black in America,” he told The New York Times earlier this year, “you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right? You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”

Bunch has worked at the Smithsonian since 1978, interrupted by stints at the California African American Museum in the 1980s and the Chicago Historical Society in the early 2000s. His tenure as secretary included the upheavals of 2020 and 2021, when—after the killing of George Floyd and amid the coronavirus pandemic—activists on the left were accusing museums across the country, including the Smithsonian, of being bastions of white privilege, colonialism, and cultural theft. Bunch remained calm and compassionate in the face of these critiques, compromising when appropriate, but never giving in to bullying.

It surely helped that his greatest achievement prior to becoming the Smithsonian’s top official was planning, raising funds for, and launching the National Museum of African American History and Culture. The museum, which opened to great fanfare in 2016, has been hugely popular. Under Bunch’s leadership, the museum balanced a forthright, profoundly moving description of slavery and its long aftereffects with exhibits that bear witness to the extraordinary flowering of African American culture, celebrating a panoply of achievements by Black Americans across many fields of human endeavor.

The Smithsonian was founded by an act of Congress in 1846. During the Civil War, it created a controversy by refusing to host a lecture series presented by abolitionists. The institution’s leadership eventually relented, but Frederick Douglass, the most prominent abolitionist of the day, was still not permitted to speak. At the 2019 ceremony installing him as secretary, Bunch referred back to those days: “Today we are here speaking in a place as an African American, where Frederick Douglass could not speak, but we are a different institution.”

Bunch’s leadership, and the Smithsonian’s resilience, has been severely tested since Trump’s return to power. Efforts by the institution to tell what Kim Sajet, the former director of the National Portrait Gallery, described as “a fuller, more American story” and “one that fosters connection, reflection and understanding” came into conflict with White House officials who felt that the “fuller story” being told was overly focused on moral failure, hypocrisy, and oppression.

The new administration was quick to target the Smithsonian. Some of what gave Bunch moral authority during the Biden years now threatened to work against him.

In March 2025, an executive order noted that the United States had witnessed “a concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history.” The Smithsonian, it stated, had, “in recent years, come under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology.” Trump announced that he was firing Sajet. The Smithsonian regents asserted that only Bunch had authority over such personnel decisions, but she resigned anyway.

More recently, the administration has ramped up pressure on the Smithsonian, demanding an overhaul of its presentations to rid them of perceived liberal bias and attempting to force its hand with explicit threats, such as pulling funding and erecting warning signs in front of the National Museum of American History. (Although it is independent, the biggest share of the institution’s budget comes from the federal government.)

Bunch has had to figure out how to handle these various assaults without allowing the Smithsonian’s mission to be compromised. He has said plenty on the public record—all of it sage and diplomatic, yet consistently firm on questions of principle. I can only imagine what private conversations he has been having on a daily basis.

Thanks to the double whammy of COVID and activist pressures, few leaders of any prominent organization have had a fun time since 2020. But Bunch has been the leader of an enormous—and enormously important—institution that’s explicitly in the business of (among other things) telling the American story at a time when the question of how to tell that story has become so fraught and divisive.

What to do in such circumstances? Perhaps Americans could all begin by just agreeing that the pandas in the National Zoo (which is part of the Smithsonian) are very, very cute. And then, perhaps, that the Apollo 11 command module in the National Air and Space Museum—the one that carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin to the moon and back—is really cool. If so, perhaps they can next agree that Bunch, during his tenure at the helm of the Smithsonian, has been the exact combination of resolute leader and compassionate and good-humored public servant that America needed him to be.
